newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Details of Russian cosmonauts' route home.
newsitem.headline: Details of Russian cosmonauts' route home.

text.p: Two Russian cosmonauts returning to Earth after arguably the toughest mission in the history of manned space flights face further tests on their way home on Thursday.
Commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin left the Mir space station on Thursday morning and entered a Soyuz spacecraft.

They will undock from the station at 12:53 (0853 GMT), Mission Control officials said, and plunge 400 km (250 miles) before landing in the steppes of the former Soviet republic of Kazakhstan at 4:16 p.m. (1216 GMT).
"During their return the cosmonauts will be dressed in lightweight spacesuits, each weighing 10 kg, with independent air supply systems," said Pyotr Klimuk, head of the Cosmonauts' Training Centre.
He said light spacesuits were introduced in 1973 after three Soviet cosmonauts -- Georgy Dobrovolsky, Vladislav Volkov and Viktor Patsayev -- died during descent in 1971 in a capsule which lost air.

"At the height of 41 km the cosmonauts will be exposed to maximum overload of 3.8 units for five minutes, which means that the weight of each cosmonaut will increase 3.8-fold," Klimuk said, adding that the pair had been prepared to face much greater overloads.
"During training they have overloads of eight units now. Earlier cosmonauts were exposed to 14 units," he said.

Brake parachutes will open at a height of 9.6 km (six miles), dragging out a huge 1,000-square-metre orange main parachute from the capsule. There is also a back-up main parachute of 574 square metres in Soyuz, Klimuk said.
On Earth, eight rescue helicopters will be in the air near the spot where the capsule is due to land.
"The cosmonauts will be helped out of the capsule. They will undergo medical checks immediately in a tent, then they will take a helicopter to Dzhezkazgan."
From there they will travel by plane to Chkalovsky military airbase near Moscow, then a bus will take them to the Star City training centre, Klimuk said.
"They may go home after seven or 10 days, but they will be able to see their families during this period," he added.
The two cosmonauts, and NASA astronaut Michael Foale, who will stay aboard Mir until September, have endured a series of major woes since they came aboard in February.
The most serious incident was a June 25 collision between Mir and its resupply ship.
